slides.say: Dan has three cards with the numbers two, five and seven. He picks two or more of the cards and multiplies their numbers. What is the sum of all the different products he can get?

So this time we don't break a number, we build numbers. Two or more cards, multiplied, and then we add up all the products. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, building every product, and then a quick look at the choices.

[short pause] Our first method. So I don't miss any, I go in order, first every pair of cards, and then all three together. Does the order of the cards matter? No, two times five and five times two are the same product, so each pair counts once.
Pairs. Two times five is ten. Two times seven is fourteen. Five times seven is thirty-five.
And now careful, two or more includes all three. A lot of students stop at the pairs. Two times five times seven, ten times seven, is seventy.

Are they all different? Yes. With different primes, every group gives its own product. Now let's add, starting from the big one. Seventy plus thirty-five is a hundred five. Plus fourteen is a hundred nineteen. Plus ten is a hundred twenty-nine. Choice number one is our answer.
at: Choice number one is our answer

slides.say: And look, if you forget the seventy, you get fifty-nine, and it's right there in the choices, choice number four. And seventy and fourteen are single products, not the sum.

[pause] Our second method, a quick look at the choices. One of the products is all three cards together, two times five times seven, seventy. And the pairs add more on top of it. So the sum is more than seventy.
Which choices are more than seventy? Only a hundred twenty-nine. Seventy, fourteen and fifty-nine are all seventy or less. So choice number one. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
